edges.description: Reduced availability of the structural subunit is expected to impair assembly; the assembly evidence comes from COX6A1 knockdown cells.
Assembly impairment is inferred from reduced subunit abundance and the knockdown model; it has not been measured for this stop-loss allele.
Impaired respiratory-chain activity can reduce oxidative ATP production; both reduced enzyme activity and ATP content were observed in patient-derived cells.

A proposed metabolic route through impaired oxidative metabolism and greater reliance on glycolysis. Lactate elevation was observed in only the stop-loss child, whose complex IV activity and metabolic flux were not reported in the accessible abstract. This is an inference across the biochemical and clinical evidence, not a measured allele-specific chain.
intermediate_mechanisms: Impaired oxidative metabolism with increased reliance on glycolysis

edges.description: The route from impaired energy metabolism to peripheral axonal injury remains unresolved; ATP and conduction measurements were made in different tissues or systems.
Loss of motor axon function can cause denervation-pattern muscle atrophy; mouse histology supports this route.

Impaired peripheral nerve function includes the observed slowing. The contributions of axonal dysfunction and myelin changes are unresolved; an axonal lesion alone is not asserted to cause the mixed pattern.

Dysfunction of distal sensory fibers provides the clinical explanation for the glove-and-stocking sensory deficit. This is a physiological inference from the sensorimotor neuropathy, not an isolated causal experiment.
Impaired afferent or efferent limbs of peripheral reflex arcs can explain absent upper-limb and ankle reflexes. Brisk knee reflexes in the same patient show that this is site-specific.
intermediate_mechanisms: Impaired peripheral afferent or efferent reflex-arc function

edges.description: Loss of effective motor-axon input can reduce distal motor-unit recruitment and force; this links the neuropathy to the documented distal weakness.
The motor neuropathy provides the physiological explanation for the severe ankle dorsiflexor deficit. The individual contribution of denervation and muscle atrophy was not quantified.
Pain was clinically attributed to the neuropathy in the Czech case. The responsible excitability or nociceptive signaling changes were not measured.
Neurogenic loss of muscle bulk manifests clinically as distal amyotrophy; the human finding and mouse neurogenic histology support this connection.
Chronic imbalance of muscle forces is a plausible route from distal weakness to the observed cavus deformity. The Czech report documents both findings but does not directly test this causal sequence.
intermediate_mechanisms: Chronic imbalance of forces acting on the foot

edges.description: Reduced ankle dorsiflexion can impair foot clearance and contribute to gait instability. This is an inferred contribution; the reported gait was not specifically classified as steppage.
